results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
**How long you have to keep tax records**

* **General rule** – Keep all records that support an item of income or deduction on a tax return **until the period of limitation for that return expires**. The period of limitation is the time during which you can amend your return or the IRS can assess additional tax. Keep a copy of each filed return as well, because it helps you prepare future returns and amend any changes if needed. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* **Employment‑tax records** – If you have employees, retain all employment‑tax records for **at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* **Asset‑related records** – Keep records related to property (e.g., for depreciation, amortization, or basis calculations) **until the period of limitation expires for the year in which the property is disposed of in a taxable transaction**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

These are the specific time‑frames given in the IRS guidance. If you need any additional clarification about your particular situation, consult the relevant IRS publication or a tax professional.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records for several practical and legal reasons:

1. **To monitor the progress of your business** – Good records let you see whether the business is improving, which items sell best, and what changes you may need to make. This can increase the likelihood of success. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

2. **To prepare accurate financial statements** – Income‑statement (profit‑and‑loss) and balance‑sheet reports can be produced only with complete records. These statements help you deal with banks or creditors and manage the business yourself. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

3. **To identify the source of receipts** – You receive money or property from many sources; records show whether an amount is business or non‑business, taxable or nontaxable, and help separate business income from personal funds. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

4. **To keep track of deductible expenses** – Recording expenses when they occur prevents you from forgetting them when you file your tax return. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

5. **To prepare your tax returns** – Your records must support the income, expenses, and credits you report. They are the same documents you use for business monitoring and financial statements. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

6. **To support items reported on tax returns** – If the IRS examines your return, you must be able to explain every item. A complete set of records speeds the examination and reduces the risk of penalties. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

7. **For federal tax purposes** – Your record‑keeping system must show gross income, deductions, and credits, and must stay in place as long as those records are “material to the administration of tax law.” Electronic or paper records are treated the same. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

8. **To keep consistent accounting methods** – Your books must use one method (cash, accrual, etc.) that clearly shows income, and you need to keep records that support that method for each business you run. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

So, by keeping thorough records you can track performance, prepare accurate statements, file taxes correctly, and satisfy tax‑authority inquiries.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 11)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 12)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
**Which accounting method should you use?** The IRS lets you choose one of several methods when you file your first tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040). The method you pick must be the one you use for both your books and for calculating taxable income, and it should fully reflect your business activity. The choice depends mainly on whether you keep inventory, how you pay and get paid, and whether you are a very small taxpayer. | Method | When it’s normally chosen | Key rules (from the IRS) | |--------|---------------------------|--------------------------| | **Cash method** | • You receive cash soon after providing services or selling goods.
• You don’t keep inventory or you are a very small business. | • Income is reported in the year you receive it.
• Most expenses are deducted or capitalized in the year you pay them.
• If you use cash for income, you must use cash for expenses.
• If you use any combination method that includes cash, the overall method is treated as cash.
• You may use cash for business income even if you keep separate books for personal items. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | | **Accrual method** | • You produce, purchase, or sell merchandise and need to track inventory.
• You bill customers and may receive payment later. | • Income is reported in the year it’s earned (even if payment comes later).
• Expenses are deducted or capitalized when incurred, not when paid.
• Inventory must be kept and accrual must be used for purchases and sales of merchandise.
• If you use accrual for expenses, you must use accrual for income.
• Near‑term exceptions exist for very small businesses that do not keep inventory. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | | **Special methods** | • You have a specific type of income/expense that the IRS allows a special rule, such as depletion, amortization, bad‑debt deduction, or installment sales. | • These apply to specific items only; you can combine them with cash or accrual for the rest of your activity.
• Examples: amortization for intangible property, depreciation for tangible property, installment sales for large asset sales, etc. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) | | **Combination method** | • You have some activities that require accrual (e.g., inventory) and others that can be tracked on cash (e.g., billings that get paid quickly). | • You may mix cash, accrual, and special methods *if* the combination clearly shows income and is used consistently.
• If the combination includes a cash component, the whole method is treated as cash.
• If inventory is required, accrual must be used for purchases and sales. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) | ### How to decide 1. **Check whether you keep inventory**. • If you *do* keep inventory (goods held for sale, raw materials, supplies that become part of merchandise), you must use the accrual method for purchases and sales of that inventory (unless you qualify for the small‑business exception). • If you *don’t* keep inventory, you may choose cash or accrual; many small businesses that have no inventory default to cash. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) 2. **Consider your cash flow**. • If you normally receive payment soon after providing services or making sales, the cash method may be simpler. • If you issue invoices and customers pay months later, the accrual method better matches income to the year it’s earned. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) 3. **Look at the size of the business**. • Very small taxpayers may qualify for the **small‑business exception** that lets you use the cash method even if you have some inventory or receive payments later. Check the current threshold in Pub. 538 or the tax code. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) 4. **Special situations**. • If you have deductible installment sales, bad‑debt situations, or other special rules, you can apply the corresponding special method to those items while using cash or accrual for the rest. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) 5. **First return requirement** • The method you pick must be declared on your **first** business tax return that includes a Schedule C. After that, changing the method generally needs IRS approval (Form 3115 or an optional automatic change if applicable). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) ### Quick guide | Situation | Recommended method | Why | |-----------|--------------------|-----| | No inventory, quick cash receipts | Cash | Simple and matches receipt with income. | | Inventory and sales to customers with later payments | Accrual | Tests require inventory and “earned but unpaid” income must be matched. | | Very small business with some inventory but below the threshold | Cash (if eligible) | Small‑business exception lets you use cash even with inventory. | | Mix of inventory and non‑inventory transactions | Combination (accrual for inventory, cash for others) | Must meet inventory rule; combination allowed if it clearly shows income. | | Special deductions (depletion, amortization, bad debts, etc.) | Apply the specific special method to the relevant items | IRS permits special treatment for certain costs. | --- **Bottom line:** Choose **cash** if you have no inventory or qualify for the small‑business exception; choose **accrual** if you keep inventory or need to match income to the year earned; use a **combination** method only when inventory rules require accrual for those items but other parts of your business are well‑served by cash. Once you file your first return, stick with that method unless you obtain IRS permission to change it. **Sources:** 1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) 2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 17)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) 3. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) 4. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards you can follow the step‑by‑step process described in the handbook:

1. **Conduct a workplace self‑inspection**  
   – The first step is to have knowledgeable and experienced workers perform a routine safety and health inspection of the actual work processes.  Small‑business owners are encouraged to do this regularly so they can *identify, control, and monitor* hazards.  This is described as the “effective way to identify workplace hazards” in the handbook.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Use the self‑inspection checklists**  
   – The handbook contains checklists that cover general‑industry workplaces.  They give you a starting point for spotting hazards.  Each checklist ends with a link to additional resources on that topic.  These checklists should be filled out by the inspectors and then compiled with injury/illness records, training logs, and equipment maintenance records.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Review OSHA standards that apply to your business**  
   – After you complete a checklist, look up the specific OSHA standards that apply to your workplace (for example, the Hazardous Materials standards for businesses that handle compressed gases, flammables, or explosives).  This helps you see whether a general‑duty clause is still needed.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)

4. **Consult available resources**  
   – If you need help interpreting the standards or finding solutions, you can use the free resources listed on OSHA’s website (publications, videos, safety‑and‑health‑topic pages) or request a visit from the **OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program**.  The program offers no‑cost, confidential help to identify hazards and how to eliminate them.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)

5. **Integrate inspections into your daily operations**  
   – The handbook stresses that safety inspections should be a routine part of everyday work, not a one‑time event.  Regular inspections help keep hazards under control and ensure that safety remains a priority.  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

6. **Keep records and follow up**  
   – After hazards are identified and controls are implemented, document the actions taken and review the effectiveness of those controls over time.  This monitoring step helps verify that hazards remain controlled.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

By following these steps—self‑inspection, using the handbook checklists, reviewing relevant OSHA standards, seeking help from the On‑Site Consultation Program, making inspections an everyday practice, and tracking results—you can systematically check your workplace for hazards and keep your workplace safe.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 8)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)
2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 91)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)
3. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 90)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)
4. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 7)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
**Cash vs. accrual accounting**

| Feature | Cash method | Accrual method |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| **When income is reported** | When you actually receive the money (or when it becomes constructively available) | When you earn the income—i.e., when the right to receive is fixed and the amount can be determined accurately | 
| **When expenses are deducted** | When the expense is paid | When the expense is incurred (the obligation exists), even if the cash is paid later |
| **Key rule for income** | “Include in your gross income all items of income you actually or constructively receive during your tax year” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | “Include an amount in your gross income for the tax year in which all events that fix your right to receive the income have occurred…and you can determine the amount with reasonable accuracy” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| **Key rule for expenses** | “Deduct an expense you pay in advance only in the year to which it applies” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) | “Deduct or capitalize expenses in the year incurred” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| **Inventory requirement** | Usually acceptable if you have no inventory, but if you must keep inventory you’re generally required to use accrual [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | “If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for purchases and sales” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) |
| **Typical businesses** | Most sole‑prop owners without inventory, or those who find cash tracking easier [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | Companies with inventory, sales‑force commissions, or other timing differences between earning and receiving money [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) |

**Bottom line**  
- **Cash** accounting matches income and expenses to the year you actually receive the money or actually pay it.  
- **Accrual** accounting matches income and expenses to the year they are earned or incurred, regardless of when cash flows happen.  

These definitions are directly taken from the IRS material in the provided segments.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)
3. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes – the IRS allows you to deduct ordinary and necessary expenses that you incur while traveling for business.  
Below is what the IRS rules say can be taken out of a business‑travel bill:

| Expense | What can be deducted | Key details |
|---------|---------------------|-------------|
| **Meals & lodging** | Cost of meals and lodging on an overnight or “long‑so‑long” business trip | You may use actual costs or the standard meal allowance.  In most cases you can claim only **50 %** of meal expenses. See Pub. 463 for limits. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Transportation to the trip** | Cost of travel by airplane, train, bus, or car from home to the destination (and between the airport/station and the hotel). | Also includes taxi, commuter‑bus, or limousine fares to/from the airport or between hotel and work sites. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Baggage & shipping** | Cost of sending baggage or needed display/sampling materials between regular and temporary work locations. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Vehicle use while away** | Operating‑and‑maintenance costs of a car or truck when traveling away from home on business.  You may choose actual expenses or the standard mileage rate (see separate rules under “Car and Truck Expenses”).  If you rent a car while away, you can deduct only the business‑use portion of the rental. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Cleaning** | Dry‑cleaning and laundry while on the business trip. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Telephone & communication** | Business calls, fax, or other communication devices used during travel. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Tips** | Tips paid for any of the above travel expenses. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Employee reimbursements** | Amounts you reimburse employees for travel and meal expenses.  How you deduct depends on whether the reimbursement is made under an accountable or non‑accountable plan. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |

In short, **yes** you can deduct business travel expenses, but you must keep the expenses ordinary, necessary, and properly substantiated.  Meals are limited to 50 % of costs (unless you use the standard allowance), and vehicle costs must be separated into business and personal portions if the vehicle is used for both.  Detailed guidance and the most current limits can be found in Publication 463 and related IRS guidance.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 41)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 40)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
An executive summary should give the reader a quick, clear snapshot of the whole plan.  It is usually only one to two paragraphs long and covers:

* A short description of your business idea  
* The amount of money you need and how it will be used  
* How much capital you have already invested or will bring in  
* A brief schedule of your main goals [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

Because many details are worked out while writing the rest of the plan, you write the executive summary last so it can be a concise overview of what you have decided. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market you should:

1. **Define your niche** – state the specific segment of the market that your product or service is designed for.  
   *“Describe your market niche; who is your best customer.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Identify the customer’s characteristics** – list the features that make them your ideal buyer.  
   *“Identify those customers and describe their characteristics.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Segment the market** – group customers by relevant criteria.   
   *Business markets might be classified by industry, company size, location, or product use/application.*  
   *Consumer markets might be segmented by demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application, or benefits sought.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Estimate size and growth potential** – use population figures, sales‑tax data, industry reports, etc., to estimate how many people or businesses fit your niche and how that number is likely to change.  
   *“Estimate the approximate size and growth potential of the target market(s) using population figures, sales tax info, industry information, etc. Estimate how much of the total market you will capture.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

By following these steps you can craft a clear, data‑driven description of the customers you want to attract and retain.



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes.  The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requires a business that serves the public to **remove all “readily‑achievable” physical barriers** that prevent people who use wheelchairs (or other mobility devices) from accessing the goods or services you provide.  “Readily‑achievable” means a barrier that can be removed or altered with relatively little cost or difficulty, and the ADA does not demand a completely universal design if the changes are not plainly feasible.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

In practice that means you need to:

* **Make the entrance accessible** – give a minimum 32‑inch opening or replace a turnstile with a 32‑inch wide gate. If a turnstile is at the front, you can either remove it or add an adjacent accessible gate.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)  
* **Provide an accessible route inside** – a clear 36‑inch wide path from the entrance to the sales floor, with a 3‑by‑3‑foot turning space at corners unless a 60‑inch turn radius is possible.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  
* **Lower counters or add an accessible section** – any service counter higher than 34 inches should have an accessible portion no higher than 34 inches long at least 60 inches.  A 30‑by‑48‑inch clearance in front of the counter lets a wheelchair user pull up.  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)  
* **Provide accessible seating if you have fixed tables** – one fixed table per 20 tables (or at least one if fewer than 20) must be at a height of 28‑34 inches with 27 inches of knee clearance.  [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)  
* **Install accessible parking** – one accessible parking space for every 25 total spaces; the space must have a 5‑ft wide access aisle and a 36‑inch wide parking area.  The parking and path to the entrance must have no steps or very steep slopes.  [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)  
* **Adjust policies** – if you have a policy that locks an accessible entrance during business hours, you must keep it unlocked or provide an accessible call box.  [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18)  

These requirements apply to any modifications, additions, or renovations you make after January 26 1992.  When a change is made, you must meet the ADA standards for that element.  [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=19)

In short, you do **not** have to convert your shop into a fully universal design if that isn’t readily achievable, but you are required to eliminate any barriers that you can remove or alter with minimal expense or difficulty.

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
You may be exempt from OSHA injury‑recordkeeping **if** either of the following applies to your business:

* **Your business had 10 or fewer workers for every month of the previous calendar year**.  Conditional on that head‑count, the employer is “partially exempt” from keeping OSHA Form 300, 301, and 300A logs, but must still provide the required annual summary and report certain severe cases. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  
* **Your business is classified in a low‑hazard industry** that is listed in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A.  Those industries are excluded from the general record‑keeping rule, though fatal or severe‑injury reporting requirements remain. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

Even if you meet one of these exemption criteria, you **must still**:

* Report **all work‑related fatalities** to OSHA within 8 hours.  
* Report **all work‑related in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye** within 24 hours.  

These reporting obligations apply to every employer, regardless of size or industry. If you have more than 10 employees or work in an industry not listed as low‑hazard, you are required to keep and submit OSHA injury records.

results.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
results.answer:
For a **small‑business owner** the documents you must keep and the periods you must keep them are listed in the IRS and OSHA guidance below.

---

## 1.  Tax‑related records  

| What to keep | Why it matters | How long to keep it | Source |
|--------------|----------------|---------------------|--------|
| **Copies of every federal tax return you file** (1040, 1040‑S, 1120, etc.) and the original return documents that back up the numbers on it. | The return is your official statement to the IRS. If the IRS ever needs to examine it, you must be able to show the supporting facts. | Keep them **as long as the period of limitation applies** – i.e., until the statute of limitations for that tax year expires. (The period of limitation is the time in which the IRS may assess additional tax or you may amend the return.)  | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Records that support each item of income or deduction** (receipts, invoices, mileage logs, etc.). | These documents must be able to prove the numbers on your return. | Keep them **as long as the period of limitation runs out** – which is the same time as the return. The IRS can audit you up to 7 years after the return was filed for most taxes. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Employment‑tax records** (payroll data, payroll‑tax returns such as Forms 941/944, payroll‑tax payments, Form W‑2s, Form W‑3, and Forms 1099). | You must prove that you withheld, deposited, and paid the correct amounts. | Keep them **at least 4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Records concerning business property** (depreciation schedules, purchase invoices, sales or disposition records). | These are needed to calculate depreciation/amortization and to determine your basis when you sell or dispose of the property. | Keep them **for as long as the period of limitation expires for the year in which you dispose of the property**. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Other supporting documents** (e.g., asset title, loan statements, bank statements) that help establish your obligations and assets. | They support the calculations that appear on your tax return. | Keep them for the same period as the tax return they support. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

**In short:** keep any document that backs up a tax return for **the full amount of time the IRS can take action** on that tax year (typically 7 years), and keep employment‑tax records for **4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**.  Any asset‑related records stay in your files until the limitation period for the year you dispose of that asset is finished. 

---

## 2.  Injury and illness records (OSHA)

| What to keep | Why it matters | How long to keep it | Source |
|--------------|----------------|---------------------|--------|
| **OSHA Form 300** (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) and the **annual summary Form 300A** | These logs are mandatory for workplaces that meet OSHA’s size or industry thresholds; they record every recordable injury/illness. | Keep them **at the worksite for at least 5 years** after the calendar year covered. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 301** (Injury and Illness Incident Report) – a supplementary report for each recordable case | Provides detailed information on each incident. | Keep alongside the Form 300 and 300A for the same 5‑year period. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker medical and exposure records** (if applicable, under 29 CFR 1910.1020) | Must be available for review and to comply with privacy and reporting regulations. | Keep for the **time period required for each specific type of record** (often 5 years, but can vary by record type). | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker training records** (that show OSHA‑required training completed by employees) | Accessible for review; demonstrates compliance with OSHA training requirements. | Keep them as long as they are needed for OSHA’s logical review, typically **the same 5‑year period**. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, loss‑of‑eye reports** | Must be reported promptly to OSHA; documentation supports those reports. | Keep these reports as part of the OSHA Form 300/300A/301 records for 5 years. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

**In short:** for OSHA, keep Forms 300/300A/301 and the associated medical, exposure, and training records for **five (5) years after the end of the calendar year that the records cover**.

---

### Summary

- **Tax records:** keep any document that supports a tax return **for the length of the applicable period‑of‑limitations** (usually 7 years after the return was filed); keep employment‑tax records **at least 4 years after the tax’s due/date



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)
2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

results.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
results.answer:
**Starting a business**

1. **Choose a legal structure** – Pick the form that fits your plans (sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, LLC, etc.). The structure decides which tax returns you’ll file and how income is reported. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  
2. **Register and get an EIN** – You’ll need an Employer Identification Number unless you are a sole proprietor who uses only a Social Security number. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  
3. **Pick a tax year** – You can adopt a calendar year (January 1 – December 31) or another fiscal year, but you must file your first return using the year you choose. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  
4. **Select an accounting method** – Use either cash or accrual, or a method that clearly shows your income for the year. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
5. **Open a business‑checking account** – Keep business and personal money separate; record every receipt and write checks from this account. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  
6. **Record daily transactions** – Use a checkbook or journal to note each expense and source of income. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

**Keeping your taxes organized**

| What to keep | How it helps | Where to find the details |
|--------------|--------------|--------------------------|
| **Books and journals** – sums of income, expenses, assets, liabilities | Allows you to prepare income‑statement and balance‑sheet reports and to file accurate returns | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Receipts, invoices, and expense slips** – source documentation | Supports the amounts reported on tax returns and protects you in an audit | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Digital copies or scans** – electronic records that are retrievable and legible at any time | Meets the IRS requirement that records be accessible in electronic form if you replace hard copy books | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Bank statements and reconciliation reports** – shows that the checkbook matches the bank record | Detects errors and prevents fraudulent entries | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Business‑related start‑up cost schedule** – list of pre‑operation expenses | Allows you to claim up to $5,000 in immediate deduction for start‑up and organizational costs; any excess must be amortized | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9) |

**Filing and paying business taxes**

1. **Federal taxes you may need to pay** – Income, self‑employment, employment taxes, and excise taxes. The exact tax and the form you use depend on your business type. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
2. **Estimated tax payments** –  
   * Sole proprietor, partner or S‑corp shareholder: pay if you expect a tax bill of $1,000 or more. Use Form 1040‑ES. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)  
   * Corporation: pay if you expect a tax bill of $500 or more. Deposit through EFTPS. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)  
3. **Deposit system** – All federal employment, excise, and corporate income taxes must be deposited electronically via EFTPS (or a trusted third party). Your EIN automatically enrolls you in EFTPS. [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8)  
4. **Tax return filing** –  
   * Sole proprietors file Form 1040 (or 1040‑SR) with a Schedule C.  
   * Partnerships file a partnership information return (Form 1065) and issue K‑1s to partners.  
   * Corporations file Form 1120 (or 1120‑S) and attach any required schedules. [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=3)  
5. **Electronic filing** – Upload forms to the IRS e‑file system; it expedites processing and reduces errors. [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=49)  
6. **Tax calendars and deadlines** – Use the IRS tax calendars (Publication 509) to locate specific due dates for each return and payment. [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

**Key facts for staying organized**

* **Separate records for each business** – If you run multiple businesses, keep a complete, separate set of books

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
To keep your employees safe and make your premises accessible, you need to meet both **workplace‑safety requirements** (OSHA‑style) and **accessibility standards** (ADA).  The handbook gives concrete, numbered items for each.

---

### 1.  Build a Safety Management Program  
* **Planning** – Identify emergencies, create evacuation routes, and designate an evacuation leader.  Use the Emergency Action Plan checklist: identify when to evacuate, who will order it, and how to assist people who need extra help.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26)  
* **Hazard identification** – Inspect walkways, ladders, and elevated surfaces regularly.  Keep walkways clean, repair holes, and provide non‑slip mats on wet surfaces.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)  
* **Ladder safety** – Maintain all ladders in good condition, use only ladder types that meet the 29 CFR 1910.23 spacing, and keep ladders away from traffic.  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=75)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=76)  
* **Elevated‑surface protection** – Guardrails for anything more than 4 ft, use safety nets or personal fall protection, and provide eye protection for workers who may be exposed to falling objects.  [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73)  
* **Workplace Violence Prevention** – Identify risk factors, record incidents, and develop a prevention plan.  [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=84)  
* **Training & Communication** – Provide workers with hazard‑identification training, conduct routine safety briefings, and document all procedures.  Use OSHA’s “Safety and Health Program” listening board as a checklist.  [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=10)  
* **Self‑inspection** – Perform regular walk‑throughs with workers, use the handbook’s self‑inspection checklists, and follow up on any identified hazards.  [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

---

### 2.  Make the Premises Accessible (ADA)

| Feature | Requirement | Source |
|---------|--------------|--------|
| **Entrance** | At least one public entrance must be accessible. If the primary entrance has a step, provide a ramp (≤ 1:12 slope), **36 in.** minimum width, or a lift. Install handrails and an edge‑protection.  Sign must direct patrons to the accessible entrance if the main one is not. | Segment 1, 6 |
| **Turnstiles** | Remove or replace non‑accessible turnstiles. If removal isn’t possible, add an accessible gate adjacent to the turnstile. The opening must be **≥ 32 in.** wide. | Segment 2 |
| **Parking** |  
- **Cars**: At least one accessible car space per 25 total spaces.  
- **Vans**: At least one per 8 accessible car spaces, and a van‑accessible space must be at least **8 ft.** wide with an **8‑ft** access aisle.  
- Minimum vertical clearance **98 in.**; slope no steeper than **1:50**. | Segments 7‑11 |
| **Counter & Checkout** | Counter height ≤ 36 in. (38 in. for checkout) with a **30 in. × 48 in.** clear floor space in front of the reachable face, and a sign with the international symbol over the aisle. | Segment 8 |
| **Shelves/Displays** | Keep a **36 in.** wide route between shelving units; provide **3‑ft × 3‑ft** turning space. Accessible aisles must be signed with the accessibility symbol. | Segment 9 |
| **Tables & Seating** | If you have fixed tables, at least **5 %** (or one if < 20) must be accessible: table height 28‑34 in., 27 in. knee clearance, and **30 in. × 48 in.** clear floor area. | Segment 18 |
| **General Barriers** | Evaluate all points of entrance, passways, and routes. Remove “readily achievable” barriers (steps, awnings, narrow aisles) and follow ADA Standards where possible; otherwise use “other” accessible methods like vehicle delivery. | Segments 5, 14, 16 |

---

### 3.  Combine Safety & Accessibility

While making ramps or accessible routes, obey safety engineering:

* **Ramps** – Minimum width **36 in.**, maximum slope 1:12, edge protection, handrails, and a wide landing.  Check for slip resistance and stable surface.  
* **Ladders and Aisles** – Use secure ladders when raising or lowering employees onto a ramp or platform; keep the clear path free of obstacles.  

By following the checklist in **Segments 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 18**, setting up a **Safety & Health Program** (Segments 19‑21) and conducting routine **self‑inspections** (Segment 25), you can keep employees protected and ensure the premises remains fully accessible to all patrons and employees.

results.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
results.answer:
**Writing a Business Plan**

1. **Cover Page** – Include your company name, address, phone, owners and their contact details, logo (if any) and the date of the plan.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

2. **Table of Contents** (optional but helpful) – List each major section and its page number.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

3. **Executive Summary** – A concise overview (1–2 paragraphs) of your idea, the capital you need, how you will use it, and a brief schedule of goals. Write this last so you can include final numbers.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

4. **Describe Your Business** – Give background, industry context, competitive positioning, and future projections.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  

5. **Describe Your Product(s)** – Marketability, purpose, uniqueness, development stage, production process, suppliers, quality control, and future offerings.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  

6. **Proprietary Information & Regulations** – Note any patents, copyrights, or trademarks and list all required licenses and regulatory bodies.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  

7. **Facilities & Equipment** – Describe location, size, equipment needs, and plans for upgrading or relocating.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  

8. **Marketing & Operations** – Explain how you will market, the marketing mix, daily operations, and staffing.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4) (general guidance)  

9. **Management & Personnel** – Identify owners, their roles, board members, staff positions, qualifications, and compensation.  
   [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13)  

10. **Financial Section** –  
    * **Historical Financials** (if any) – past income statements, balance sheets, cash flows.  
    * **Financial Projections** – 3‑year income projections with monthly detail, cash‑flow projections, and a balance sheet.  
    * **Money Section** – Summarize total financial need, equity invested, and sources‑and‑uses.  
    * **Sources & Uses Statement** – List each use of capital and the corresponding source.  
    * **Notes & Critical Assumptions** – Explain assumptions behind revenue, expenses, and other key numbers.  
    [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=17)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=20)  

11. **Appendices** – Including credit reports, leases, contracts, and any supporting documents.  
    [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=17)  

**Setting Up Accounting (Bookkeeping & Record‑Keeping)**

1. **Choose a Business Checking Account** – Separate from personal funds; deposit all daily receipts; note source and type of each deposit on the slip.  
   [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

2. **Record Transactions Promptly** –  
   * Record expenses as they occur; identify the receipt source.  
   * Make payments by check; write checks payable to yourself only for withdrawals.  
   * Keep copies of all slips and receipts; note cash payments in the records.  
   [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

3. **Select an Accounting Method** –  
   * **Cash** – Income when received, expense when paid.  
   * **Accrual** – Income when earned, expense when incurred.  
   * **Special or Combination** may be used for specific items or mix of methods.  
   Once chosen, use it consistently for taxes and books.  
   [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

4. **Determine a Bookkeeping System** –  
   * **Single‑Entry** – Simple cash‑flow log: daily cash receipts and monthly summaries.  
   * **Double‑Entry** – Journal entries posted to ledgers, with debits and credits balancing.  
   Choose based on your business size and complexity.  
   [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  

5. **Set Up Journals & Ledgers** –  
   * **Business Checkbook** – Main source of entries.  
   * **Daily Cash Receipts Summary** – For daily entries.  
   * **Monthly Cash Receipts & Disbursements** – Review each month.  
   * **Check Disbursements Journal** – Record each drawn check, including number, payee, and amount.  
   * **Depreciation Worksheet** – For capital assets.  
   * **Employee Compensation Record** – Pay, taxes, benefits.  
   [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  

6. **Reconcile Regularly** – When you receive a bank statement, compare it with your checkbook, journals, and ledgers to ensure they all match.  
   [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

7. **Maintain Supporting Documents** – Keep all receipts, invoices, contracts, and other evidence that backs up your entries. All records must be available for IRS inspection.  
   [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

8. **Electronic Record‑Keeping** – If you use electronic imaging or backups, keep them legible and accessible, and maintain them as long as they are material for tax purposes.  
   [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

9. **Other Tax‑Related Set‑Up** –  
   * Obtain an EIN if you will hire employees or pay Federal Excise Tax.  
   * File a presumed business name (fictitious name) if required.  
   [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  

**Quick Checklist**  
| Task | Key Segment |
|------|-------------|
| Include cover page, table of contents, executive summary | Segment 1 |
| Collect financial history, projections, and sources‑and‑uses | Segments 3, 12 |
| Outline products, market, competition, operations, management | Segments 7, 11 |
| Separate business checking account | Segment 2 |
| Record daily transactions, document receipts | Segment 2 |
| Choose cash or accrual accounting

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
The segments do provide information that allows you to answer the question.  

**Do you need an EIN?**  
You need an Employer Identification Number (EIN) under the following circumstances:  
* if you hire employees — or have a payroll to run [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
* if you file certain federal tax returns such as payroll, excise, or certain excise tax returns [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
* many business structures (partnerships, LLCs, corporations) are required to obtain an EIN, and a sole‑proprietor may choose to get one to keep the owner’s Social‑Security number separate from the business ID [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)  
If you are a sole proprietor with no employees and you are happy to use your Social‑Security number for all federal filings, you could optionally skip the EIN, but many IRS publications recommend it so the business has a distinct taxpayer ID [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4).

**What accounting method goes with an EIN?**  
An EIN itself does not “come with” a particular accounting method.  
When you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (or other business form), you must choose an accounting method—cash, accrual, or a combination that clearly shows income [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  
You can use the same method for all purposes (tax, bookkeeping, and reporting) and you must keep records that make the method clear. The choice is independent of whether you have an EIN.  

So:  
* You likely need an EIN if you have employees or any of the business structures listed above.  
* The accounting method is chosen when you file your first return and it is not dictated by having an EIN.  

These statements are drawn from the excerpts in Segments 1, 2, 3, and 4.

results.question: why should i bother with a safety program and what records do i need to keep
results.answer:
Because a safety program is more than a box‑check exercise – it protects the people who run your business, keeps the business running smoothly, and helps you avoid costly surprises.

**Why a safety program matters**  
- It keeps workers from injuries, illnesses, and deaths, which saves money, protects families and keeps the business operating – a “safe business is a sound business.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6)  
- It shifts the focus from fixing problems after they happen to finding and eliminating hazards first, which is far more effective and less disruptive. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  
- It lets you demonstrate “good faith and commitment” to OSHA, making it easier to work with consultants, insurers and regulators, and often reduces costs such as workers’ compensation. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  
- OSHA’s records, reports, and inspections confirm that you’ve done your due diligence and can help avoid penalties and litigation. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  

**What records you must keep**

| Record type | What it covers | How long to keep | Where to file | Key deadlines |
|-------------|---------------|-----------------|---------------|---------------|
| **OSHA Form 300 – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses** | Every injury or illness that is not a simple first‑aid case | At least 5 years | On‑site (paper or electronic) |  |
| **OSHA Form 301 – Injury and Illness Incident Report** | Detailed incident information for each recordable case | At least 5 years | On‑site (paper or electronic) |  |
| **OSHA Form 300A – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses** | Annual summary prepared from Forms 300 and 301 | At least 5 years | On‑site (paper or electronic) | Submit electronically by **March 2 of the year after** the calendar year covered, if you have 100 or more workers in a high‑hazard industry. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) |
| **Fatality, hospitalization, amputation, or eye‑loss reports** | Must be reported to OSHA immediately | Retain the original report and corrective‑action summary for as long as the OSHA record‑keeping period (5 years) | On‑site | Report within **8 hours** for fatalities; within **24 hours** for hospitalizations, amputations, or loss of an eye. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker medical and exposure records** | Records required in the industry (e.g., exposure logs, medical evaluations) | Retain for the period required by the specific record (usually as long as the employee is exposed) | On‑site (paper or electronic) | As required by 29 CFR 1910.1020. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker training records** | Proof that employees received the required safety and health training | Keep these records at the worksite and make them accessible to workers | On‑site (paper or electronic) | As required by the relevant OSHA standard. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

**Other useful records**  
- Hazard identification and assessment logs, safety inspection checklists, and near‑miss reports can help you spot trends and design prevention measures (see Segment 8 for the business‑side view of keeping all records).  
- If you participate in OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation or Safety & Health Achievement Recognition Program, keep the consultant reports and safety‑achievement certificates. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)  
- For high‑risk industries that have special recording rules, be sure to check 29 CFR Part 1904 or the corresponding state‑plan guidance. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)  

**Bottom line**  
A safety program helps you avoid fatal accidents, keeps you compliant with OSHA reporting laws, and saves money on insurance and lost‑time costs. The records listed above are the ones required by OSHA, and keeping them for the proper time and in the proper place lets you prove you’re doing the right thing if an inspection or claim comes through.

results.question: how do i register a trademark
results.answer:
To register a trademark you can choose either a state‑level or a federal filing.  
The basic steps are:

1. **Decide the level of protection** –  
   * State‑level registration gives you exclusive rights within the state you file.  
   * Federal registration (via the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, USPTO) gives you nationwide rights.  

2. **Check if the mark is available** – Search the relevant trademark databases (state database or the USPTO’s TESS system) to make sure no identical or confusingly similar mark is already registered.  

3. **Prepare and file the application** –  
   * For a state filing, submit an application to the Secretary of State office in the state where you want protection.  
   * For a federal filing, submit an application to the USPTO.  

4. **Pay the filing fee** – Each jurisdiction sets its own fee schedule (the USPTO has standard fees listed on its website).  

5. **Wait for examination** – The office will review the application. If issues are found, you’ll receive a correspondence (office action) with instructions on how to proceed.  

6. **Publication and registration** – If the USPTO accepts the application, the mark is published in the *Trademark Official Gazette* and, after the opposition period expires without complaint, the trademark is registered. For a state filing, the Office of the Secretary of State will issue a registration certificate.

**Contacts**

* Secretary of State (state filing) – (605) 773‑2797 or https://sdsos.gov/  
* U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (federal filing) – (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199; https://www.uspto.gov  

These are the actionable steps and contact points for registering a trademark.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
You should keep your tax records:

- **For ordinary income‑tax purposes** – Keep the records that support any item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitation for that return expires. That is, keep them until the time in which you could amend the return to claim a credit or refund, or until the IRS could assess additional tax. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Employment‑tax records** – If you have employees, keep all employment‑tax records for at least **4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Asset‑related records** – Keep records relating to property until the period of limitation expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition, so you can calculate depreciation, amortization, or any gain or loss. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
You need to keep business records because they serve several essential purposes for your business and for the IRS:

- **Help you monitor your business’s progress** – records show whether the business is improving, which items sell best, and what changes are needed. This increases the likelihood of success. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
- **Enable accurate preparation of financial statements** – income (profit‑and‑loss) statements and balance sheets rely on good records. These statements are used when dealing with banks or creditors and help manage the business. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
- **Identify the source of receipts** – you need to separate business from non‑business receipts and distinguish taxable from non‑taxable income. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
- **Track deductible expenses** – if you record expenses when they occur, you are less likely to forget them when preparing tax returns. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
- **Prepare tax returns** – records must support the income, expenses, and credits you report. They are the same records used to monitor the business and prepare statements. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
- **Support items reported on tax returns** – should the IRS examine any activity, having a complete set of records available speeds the examination. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

Therefore, keeping organized, timely records is vital for business management, financial reporting, and compliance with tax requirements.



**Sources:**

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
You can pick one of the accounting methods that the IRS allows and then keep your books and tax return consistent with that choice. The basic options are:

| Method | How it reports income | How it reports expenses | When to use it | Key restrictions |
|--------|----------------------|------------------------|----------------|------------------|
| **Cash** | Income is recorded in the year you receive cash. | Expenses are usually deducted in the year you actually pay. | Simple for many sole‑proprietors or small businesses that don’t hold inventory. | If you have an inventory that must be valued, you **must** use an accrual method for purchases and sales. Otherwise you can use cash for all items. |  
| **Accrual** | Income is recorded in the year it is earned, even if payment comes later. | Expenses are deducted in the year they are incurred, regardless of payment. | Best for businesses that produce, purchase, or sell merchandise (inventory) or have significant receivables/payables. | If you use accrual for expenses, you must use accrual for income; if you mix cash for some items, the combination is treated as cash. |  
| **Combination** | May mix cash and accrual for different items. | Must consistently apply the same mix each year and the mix must clearly show income. | Useful when some parts of the business have inventory (require accrual) but other parts are purely cash‑basis. | If the mix includes any cash‑basis items, the whole method is treated as cash‑basis for reporting entries. |  
| **Special methods** | e.g., amortization, depreciation, bad‑debts, depletion, installment sales, long‑term contract methods. | Apply to specific items of income or expense only. | Use when the statutory rules require them or if they give tax benefits for particular items. | They can be used in addition to a general cash or accrual method. |

**When you make the choice**  
* You select an accounting method when you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  
* After that, any change requires IRS approval (Form 3115) unless the change is an automatic procedure. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)  

**Inventory rule**  
If your business produces, purchases, or sells merchandise, you normally must keep an inventory and use an accrual method for purchases and sales, even if you use cash for all other items. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

**Practical tip**  
*If you’re a small business with no inventory and most cash flows come in and out together, the cash method is usually simpler.*  
*If you have inventory, receivables, or want to match income and expenses more closely, the accrual method is required.*  

These are the options and conditions that the IRS documents give you to decide which accounting method to use.

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards you can follow a step‑by‑step approach that the handbook outlines for small businesses.  
The process is deliberately simple, routine, and relies on tools that are already in the handbook.  

---

### 1. **Establish a Safety and Health Program**

* Make sure you have a written safety and health program that is **used daily** and gives workers a voice.  
* The program should include **regular inspections** and procedures for workers to report hazards.  
* This is covered in the handbook’s chapters on safety programs and is a prerequisite for the inspection steps that follow.  

---

### 2. **Conduct Routine Workplace Self‑Inspections**

1. **Schedule routine checks** – at least once a month, but more often for high‑hazard tasks.  
2. **Use the self‑inspection checklists** that the handbook supplies.  
   * These checklists are designed for “general industry” workplaces (excluding construction or maritime).  
   * They give you a *starting point* for spotting hazards such as spills, unguarded machinery, inadequate lighting, or tripping hazards.  
   * They are not a compliance audit for OSHA standards but a safety‑awareness tool. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  
3. **Involve knowledgeable workers** – people who work directly with the processes are best positioned to spot hidden dangers.  
   * The handbook says “the only way to know if potential hazards exist and if they are under control is to assess work processes directly.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

---

### 3. **Compile Supporting Information**

While you conduct the walk‑through, gather:

| What to collect | Why it matters |
|-----------------|----------------|
| Completed checklist results | Shows whether hazards were found and tracked |
| Injury/illness logs (OSHA 300) | Indicates where problems have already occurred |
| Training records | Confirms workers know what to look for and how to handle hazards |
| Maintenance logs / equipment failure reports | Helps identify recurring equipment‑related risks |
| Process and equipment drawings | Provides context for evaluating control measures |

The handbook encourages combining all these records to “determine where challenges exist” and find solutions. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

---

### 4. **Identify Hazards and Controls**

For each hazard you find:

1. **Document the hazard** – describe the nature of the risk, how it can occur, and the potential outcome.  
2. **Check if a control is already in place.**  
   * If yes, assess whether it’s still effective (e.g., guarding, ventilation, PPE).  
   * If no, plan an immediate corrective action or a longer‑term solution.  
3. **Use OSHA standard references** when applicable.  
   * Review which OSHA subparts apply (e.g., Subpart H for hazardous materials).  
   * The handbook says to “review the OSHA standards to identify those that apply to your business” and to consult resources if unsure. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)  

---

### 5. **Take Corrective Action**

* **Quick fixes** – flip a toggle switch, seal a hole, remove tripping objects.  
* **Long‑term controls** – engineering controls (guards, enclosure), administrative controls (job rotation, training), PPE.  
* **Record the action** – note what was done, who did it, and when it will be re‑checked.  

---

### 6. **Maintain Records and Follow‑Up**

* Keep a log of all inspections and actions taken.  
* Review the records at the next safety meeting; let workers see the outcome of their reporting.  
* Re‑inspect the area within a reasonable time frame to confirm the hazard has been removed or mitigated.  

---

### 7. **Utilise External Resources (Optional but Helpful)**

* **OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program** – free, confidential experts can help you conduct a thorough hazard assessment or train employees. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)  
* **State Plan resources** if you’re in a state with a state‑approved OSHA plan. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=94)  
* **NIOSH resources** for more information on specific hazards. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=94)  

---

## Quick Checklist Summary

| Step | Key Action | Where to Find Tool |
|------|------------|-------------------|
| 1 | Set up safety program | Handbook safety‐program sections |
| 2 | Schedule self‑inspections | Self‑Inspection checklists in the handbook |
| 3 | Attach supportive records | Safety & health records, OSHA 300 |
| 4 | Identify and categorize hazards | Inspection checklist + OSHA standards |
| 5 | Implement controls | Plan, assign responsibility, log actions |
| 6 | Record and review | Logbook, safety meetings |
| 7 | Seek outside help if needed | OSHA On‑Site Consultation, State Plan |  

Following these steps will give you a clear, documented picture of hazards in your workplace and a plan for keeping your workers safe.



**Sources:**

2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 91)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)
