runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash or accrual accounting are the two basic rules that tell a business when it must record its income and its expenses.

| Feature | Cash method | Accrual method |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| **When income is counted** | When it is actually **received** (or “constructively” received), i.e., when the money is credited to an account or made available without restriction. | When it is earned – when all events that fix the right to the income have occurred, and the amount can be reasonably determined (the “all‑events” test). |
| **When expenses are counted** | When the money is **paid** (or can be deducted only for the year the payment is made, for pre‑paid expenses). | When the expense is **incurred**, i.e., when the obligation is fixed—even if the payment is made later. |
| **Inventory rule** | If a business must keep inventory, it is **generally required to use the accrual method** for purchases and sales. | No special inventory rule; the method is the same as for other businesses. |
| **Constructive receipt** (cash method) | If the amount is credited to your account or made available without restriction, it is treated as received. Example: you get interest credited in December 2025; you must include it in 2025 income even if you do not withdraw it until 2026. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **All‑events test** (accrual method) | Not applicable. | Under accrual you include an item in income when the right to receive it is fixed and the amount can be reasonably determined. Example: you sell a computer on Dec 28 2025, bill in early Jan 2026, and collect in Feb 2026; you must still count the sale in 2025 income. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| **Typical users** | Many sole‑proprietors and small business owners without inventory find it simpler. | Larger businesses, or those that keep inventory, use it to match income with related expenses. |
| **Choosing the method** | Pick when you file your first tax return; you can file for an extension, an EIN, and paid estimated taxes before choosing. | Same timing as cash; choose to best reflect your business operations. |
| **Changing the method** | Not covered in the segments. | Not covered in the segments. |

**Bottom line:**  
- **Cash accounting** reports money when you **get** it and expenses when you **pay** it.  
- **Accrual accounting** reports money when you **earn** it (or the obligation is fixed) and expenses when you **incur** them, even if no cash changes hands that year.  

These rules help the IRS match income and expenses to the correct tax year. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes. The IRS lets you write off the costs that are part of a bona‑fide business trip. The key points that appear in the provided segments are: | What you can deduct | How it’s calculated | Source segment | |---------------------|---------------------|----------------| | **Travel by plane, train, bus or car between home and a temporary work place** | Deduct the actual cost of the trip, or use the *standard mileage rate* for a car if you choose the simplified method. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) | | **Taxi, commuter bus, limousine, or other transit between airports/stations and your hotel or between the hotel and a job site** | Deduct the fare. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) | | **Baggage and shipping of items needed for work between your regular and temporary locations** | Deduct the shipping or baggage fees. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) | | **Car or truck operating costs when you travel away from home** | Deduct actual vehicle expenses (gas, oil, insurance, parking, tolls, etc.) *or* use the standard mileage rate, multiplied by the number of business miles. If you use the standard rate you cannot separately deduct insurance premium expenses. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) | | **Meals and lodging for overnight trips** | • If you stay overnight or for a long enough period that you must rest to perform your job, you may deduct the cost of meals and lodging.
• You may calculate your deduction using actual expenses **or** the standard meal allowance (see Pub. 463). In most cases you can deduct only **50 % of the cost of meals**.
• All meal expenses must be “ordinary and necessary.” | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) | | **Cleaning (dry‑cleaning, laundry) during a business trip** | Deduct the cost. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) | | **Telephone or fax calls made while traveling** | Deduct the cost. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) | | **Tips for services you pay on the trip** | Deduct the tips. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) | | **Reimbursement of employees** | If you reimburse employees for these travel expenses, you generally deduct the reimbursement. The exact treatment depends on whether the reimbursement is under an accountable or non‑accountable plan (see Pub. 15). | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) | ### How to determine what counts as “business use” * You must be **away from your “tax home”** (the city or the area where you normally work) **substantially longer** than a normal day and you must need to sleep or rest to perform your job, or the trip is for visiting clients, attending meetings, or similar business purposes. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) | ### Summary - Yes, you can deduct business‑related travel expenses. - Deduct actual costs for transportation, lodging, meals (50 % of meal cost), cleaning, phone, tips, and employee reimbursements, or use the standard mileage rate for car use. - Keep records that show the purpose of the trip and the expenses incurred. These provisions cover all the elements mentioned in the question and are drawn directly from the provided context segments. **Sources:** 1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 40)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) 2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 11)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) 3. runs.question: what goes in an executive summary
runs.answer:
An executive summary is a concise, one‑ to two‑paragraph overview that tells the reader what you want to achieve with the business. It should briefly cover:

* The core idea or product/service of the business  
* How much capital you need, what you will use it for, and how much you have already invested or plan to bring in  
* A short timeline or schedule of key goals and milestones  

Because some details (like exact figures or final timelines) may only be known after the rest of the business plan is finished, the executive summary is usually written last. This keeps the summary accurate and reflective of the completed plan.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
To describe your target market, follow the steps laid out in the planning guide:

1. **Define the niche and the “best” customer** – state the specific part of the overall market that your business will serve best.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Identify customer characteristics** – describe who those customers are.  
   • If you sell to other businesses, segment by industry, company size, location, or how the product is used.  
   • If you sell to consumers, segment by demographics such as age or gender, geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product use, or benefits sought.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Estimate the market size and growth potential** – use population data, sales tax information, industry reports, or other relevant data to gauge how large the market is and how fast it is expanding.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Project your market share** – estimate what percentage of that total market you expect to capture with your product or service.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

These steps give you a concise, data‑driven profile of the people or businesses most likely to buy what you offer.

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
**Do you have to make your shop wheelchair‑accessible?**  
Yes. Because your shop serves the public, the ADA requires you to eliminate any physical barriers that are “readily achievable” and to provide an accessible entrance and route into the business.  

1. **Barrier removal obligation** – “If you own or operate a business that serves the public you must remove physical “barriers” that are “readily achievable.”” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
2. **Accessible entrance** – “Providing physical access to a facility from public sidewalks, public transportation or parking is basic to making goods and services available to people with disabilities.” and “If one entrance is not accessible and another is, a sign must provide direction to the accessible entrance.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  
3. **Accessible route through the store** – “The business must provide an accessible route to fixed shelves and displays, if doing so is readily achievable.” and details on width and turning space for wheelchair maneuvering. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  
4. **Sales and service counters** – If a counter is higher than 34 in, a lowered section or an alternative accessible table must be provided. “If it is not readily achievable to make the counter accessible, a business can serve the items at nearby accessible tables, if readily achievable.” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  
5. **Parking** – If you provide public parking, an accessible space with an access aisle and a visible sign must be available. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9)  

**What “readily achievable” means** – The ADA allows a less‑strict approach for older buildings. If your shop was built before the 1993‑2002 cut‑off dates, some barriers that are expensive or technically difficult may be acceptable if they can’t be removed without undue hardship. This is covered in the discussion of “readily achievable” in segments 2 and 15.  

**Bottom line**  
For a public shop, you must (1) provide at least one accessible entrance and route, (2) keep aisles and counter heights within the ADA limits if possible, (3) keep at least one accessible parking spot, and (4) make any other “readily achievable” barriers removable. If you can’t meet all of those requirements, you must at least offer an alternative means of service (e.g., off‑site pickup or delivery).  

If you’re unsure how to apply these rules to your specific layout, the ADA Information Line (800‑514‑0301) can give you hands‑on guidance. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=19)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=5)

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
Yes. OSHA’s record‑keeping rules give partial exemptions. An employer is exempt from keeping OSHA Forms 300 (Log) and 301 (Incident Report) if:

* **The employer had 10 or fewer employees at every point during the entire previous calendar year.** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  
* **The employer works in a low‑hazard industry listed in 29 CFR Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A.** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

Even if exempt from logging injuries and illnesses, the employer must still:

* Report all work‑related **fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye** within the required time frames (8 hr for fatalities; 24 hr for the others). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

runs.answer:
You must keep OSHA injury and illness records (OSHA Form 300, Form 301, and the summary Form 300A) at the worksite for **at least five years**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
runs.answer:
**Tax records**

| What to keep | How long to keep (what the IRS says) | Source |
|--------------|----------------------------------------|--------|
| Copies of every filed tax return and the supporting schedules or statements that justify the numbers on the return | Until the period of limitations for that return expires (the IRS can still assess tax or you can amend the return during that period). In most cases that means **up to 7 years** from the original filing date. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Employment‑tax** records (payroll, W‑2s, Form 940, Form 941, FUTA, payroll‑tax calculations, etc.). | **At least 4 years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Asset‑related records (purchase invoices, basis, depreciation, sale documents). | Keep until the period of limitations expires for the year you dispose of the property, because you need them to determine gain/loss and depreciation basis. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Electronic copies that replace hard‑copy books | Must be kept for as long as they are still material to the administration of tax law, and must be accessible and legible to the IRS. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) |

**Injury/illness records**

| What to keep | How long to keep | Source |
|--------------|------------------|--------|
| OSHA **Form 300** (log of work‑related injuries/illnesses) and the corresponding **Form 301** (incident reports) | **5 years** at the worksite | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| Annual summary **OSHA Form 300A** | Same 5‑year retention as Form 300 | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) |
| Employee medical and exposure records | As long as required for that specific type of record (varies by medical condition type; see 29 CFR 1910.1020). | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| OSHA reports for fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, loss of eye | Must be submitted to OSHA within 8 hours for fatalities, 24 hours for hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of eye. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) |
| Annual electronic submission to OSHA | By **March 2** of the year after the calendar year covered | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

---

**Bottom line:**  
- Keep **all tax‑related books and supporting documents** for the length of the applicable period of limitation (usually 7 years, 4 years for employment‑tax records, and longer for assets).  
- Keep **OSHA injury/illness logs and medical records** on hand for **five years** and file the required annual summaries and reports on time.  

These rules come straight from the IRS and OSHA guidance in the supplied segments.

runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
**How to start a business and keep your taxes organized**

1. **Choose a legal form for your business**  
   * Determine whether you will operate as a sole proprietorship, partnership, or corporation, and how that choice will affect the tax forms you file. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  
   * The type of entity will decide whether you need an Employer Identification Number (EIN), a tax year, and which federal tax returns to file. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)

2. **Get a taxpayer identification number**  
   * Most businesses need an EIN; only a single‑person owner who uses a sole‑prop form and does not keep employees may use a Social‑Security number. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)

3. **Pick a tax year and an accounting method**  
   * Decide whether you will use a calendar year (Jan 1–Dec 31) or a fiscal year that begins on any month‑first date. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  
   * Choose either cash or accrual bookkeeping (or double‑entry vs. single‑entry), in a way that makes your income clearly visible for tax purposes. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

4. **Open a separate business bank account / checkbook**  
   * Record all receipts and expenditures in a business checking account; reconcile the account against your books daily or weekly. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  
   * Pay all business expenses by check (unless you write to “cash” you must keep a receipt) and note the source on the deposit slip. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

5. **Set up an accurate record‑keeping system**  
   * Use journals and ledgers (double‑entry) or a simple daily summary of cash receipts (single‑entry). [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  
   * Keep supporting documents (receipts, invoices, bank statements) at all times so you can answer an IRS question or audit. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
   * If you use electronic records, maintain them as legibly as the paper originals. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
   * If you change your accounting method, request IRS approval. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

6. **Track deductible expenses**  
   * Ordinary and necessary expenses—such as rent, utilities, supplies, advertising, and business‑bad‑debt—can be deducted on Schedule C (Form 1040) or the appropriate partnership/ corporate return. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)  
   * Start‑up costs up to $5,000 (and organizational costs up to $5,000) can be deducted this year, with any excess amortized. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)  

7. **File the correct tax returns**  
   * Sole proprietors file Schedule C (or F) with Form 1040; partnerships file Form 1065; corporations file Form 1120 (or 1120‑S). [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=3)  
   * If you have self‑employment income, attach Schedule SE (Form 1040). [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=47)  
   * Use the forms listed in the tax‑calendar tables to know the exact due dates for each type of tax. [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

8. **Pay estimated taxes if required**  
   * If you expect to owe $1,000 or more in tax, file Form 1040‑ES quarterly. Corporations pay using Form 1120‑S (or 1120) if $500 or more is expected. [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)  

9. **Deposit employment and excise taxes electronically**  
   * All federal employment taxes, excise taxes, and corporate income tax must be deposited via EFTPS (Electronic Federal Tax Payment System). [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8)  

10. **Maintain records for at least 3–7 years**  
    * The IRS may audit you up to 7 years after the year for which you filed. Keep books, receipts, and supporting documents that prove income, expenses, and deductions. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

**Summary**

1. Pick the entity type → obtain EIN → choose tax year & accounting method.  
2. Open a business bank account, record transactions daily, keep receipts, and maintain a complete book of accounts.  
3. Track ordinary and necessary expenses; deduct start‑up and organizational costs.  
4. File the correct federal return (1040 w/ Schedule C/F or partnership/ corporate return), file estimated tax if needed, and deposit employment/taxes via EFTPS.  
5. Keep all records accessible for 3–7 years for IRS inspections.  

These steps are drawn directly from the IRS guidance in the provided segments.



**Sources:**

runs.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
runs.answer:
**How to write a business plan**  

1. **Cover Page** – Include the company name, address, phone number, owners and their contact details, and the date of the plan. Add a logo if you have one. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

2. **Table of Contents (optional)** – List the sections of the plan for quick reference. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

3. **Executive Summary** – Write one‑ or two‑paragraph overview: describe the business idea, the amount of capital you need, how you will use it, and a brief schedule of milestones. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

4. **Business Description** – Explain what the business does, its history, its industry, and its future projections. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  

5. **Products / Services** – Describe each offering, its marketability, unique selling points, development stage, supplier details, and quality standards. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  

6. **Market Analysis** – Detail the target market, size, growth, segmentation, and competition. Embed this analysis into the “Describe Your Business” and “Describe Your Product(s)” sections. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  

7. **Marketing & Sales Plan** – Outline how you will attract and retain customers, pricing strategy, distribution channels, and promotional tactics. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  

8. **Operations Plan** – Describe facilities, equipment, inventory, suppliers, and day‑to‑day production or service delivery. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  

9. **Organization & Management** – State the chosen business form, list owners and ownership percentages, describe management duties, and include resumes or CVs if relevant. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13)  

10. **Personnel** – Provide expected employee numbers, job titles, responsibilities, and compensation structure. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13)  

11. **Financial Section**  
    * **Summary of Financial Need** – List total capital required, including working capital, and explain equity invested. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  
    * **Three‑Year Income Projection** – Project monthly revenue and expenses for the next 36 months, based on industry trends and your market analysis. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  
    * **Statement of Cash Flow** – Show expected cash inflows and outflows over three years, including payment terms for customers and vendors. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  
    * **Balance Sheet** – Provide the assets, liabilities, and equity snapshot as of a specified date. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  

12. **Appendices** – Attach financial schedules, resumes, lease agreements, contracts, credit reports, and any other supporting documents. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=17)  

---

**How to set up accounting for your new business**  

1. **Choose a legal structure and get a taxpayer ID** – Decide between sole‑proprietorship, partnership, LLC, corporation, etc., and obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN). [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  

2. **Open a dedicated business checking account** – Keep business and personal funds separate; deposit all daily receipts into this account, and note the source on each deposit slip or check. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

3. **Record transactions promptly** –  
   * Write checks from the business account for all expenses.  
   * If you must pay “cash,” attach the receipt or provide an adequate explanation in your records.  
   * Keep copies of all slips and receipts. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

4. **Choose an accounting method** – Decide whether to use the cash method or an accrual method (or a combination). The method must be used consistently for tax reporting and bookkeeping, and changing it later requires IRS approval. [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

5. **Pick a bookkeeping system** –  
   * **Single‑entry** (income‑statement‑only): record daily cash receipts and monthly summaries.  
   * **Double‑entry** (journals and ledgers): each transaction is recorded as a debit in one account and a credit in another, keeping the books in balance. [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  

6. **Set up journals and ledgers** –  
   * Create a **checkbook** or **business checking ledger** for cash movements.  
   * Maintain a **check disbursements journal** for all checks drawn on the business account.  
   * Keep a **cash receipts journal** (daily and monthly summaries) for receipts.  
   * Optionally hold a **depreciation worksheet** and an **employee compensation record**. [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  

7. **Reconcile the bank account** – When you receive a statement, compare it with your checkbook and journals to ensure all entries match and errors are corrected. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
runs.answer:
For a reliable tax return and for claiming travel deductions you should keep detailed records of every business‑related expense. The IRS requires you to be able to prove the amount, the date, and the business purpose of each item.

**1. General tax‑tracking records**  
* Keep a copy of every receipt, canceled check, money‑order copy, or bank‑statement entry that shows the amount you paid and that the payment was for a business purpose, so you can prove the expense when it is reported on a return or audited.*  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

* Record the date, amount, vendor, and type of each transaction in a log or accounting system that distinguishes business from personal payments.*  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

* For a sole‑proprietor, place the total of each month’s receipts and expenses in an annual summary that feeds into Schedule C (Form 1040).  This summary should include separate columns for materials, supplies, wages, rents, taxes, and other deductible costs.  The summary is then entered in Part I (income) and Part II (expenses) of Schedule C.*  
[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=17)

**2. Travel‑expense tracking**  
When you travel for business you must show that the trip was ordinary, necessary, and away from your “tax home.”  The key items to track are:

| Item | What to record | How to record |
|------|----------------|----------------|
| **Transportation** | Airfare, train, rideshare, rental‑car cost, taxi fare, mileage when using your own car | Keep the ticket or rental agreement; for own car keep a mileage log with dates, purpose, and miles counted (starting mileage at the beginning of the trip and ending mileage at the end). |
| **Lodging** | Hotels, motels, Airbnb, or any overnight stay | Keep the receipt; note city and dates. |
| **Meals** | Food and beverages while traveling | Keep the receipt; note that the meal is part of a business trip.  You may deduct only 50 % of meal expenses unless the trip is exempt (e.g., congress, audited) and you have special proof.  You may alternatively use the standard meal allowance stated in Pub. 463.  The expense must be ordinary and necessary. | 
[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2) [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13) |
| **Parking & tolls** | Parking fees and toll payments | Keep receipts or toll‑bill statements. |
| **Tips** | Gratuities given to service workers (e.g., hotel staff, drivers) | Keep the tip receipt or recall a written note if it was cash. |
| **Other incidentals** | Laundry, dry‑cleaning, telephone fees for business calls while traveling | Keep the bill, receipt, or credit‑card statement bearing the business purpose. |

**3. Special rules for travel reimbursement**  
If you reimburse employees for travel or meal costs, record whether the reimbursement is made under an accountable plan or a non‑accountable one, and retain the supporting documents (reimbursement forms, receipts).  The rules for reporting these reimbursements affect how you deduct the amounts on your return.  
[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

**4. Summary**  
Track a complete set of documents that cover every dollar you spend:  

* receipts and invoices (business supplies, rent, utilities)  
* canceled checks or bank‑statement lines (salary, rent, taxes)  
* mileage log for personal vehicles (dates, purpose, miles)  
* lodging and meals receipts (food cost, 50 % rule)  
* transportation receipts (airfare, rental, taxi/tolls)  
* parking and toll receipts  
* tips and incidentals (laundry, telephone)  

Keep all of the above five months at least as long as required by IRS record‑keeping rules (generally 3–7 years), as they may be needed to support the deductions you claim on your return.  

If you have more specific questions about a particular type of travel expense, let me know – the same recording principles apply.

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
Yes.  

**1. Do you need an EIN?**  
* If you have employees, if you form a corporation, partnership, or a multi‑member LLC (or elect to treat a single‑member LLC as a corporation), you **must obtain an EIN**.  
* Even a sole‑proprietor who does not have employees may need an EIN if the IRS requires it for certain filings (e.g., filing payroll taxes).  
* You can obtain an EIN online, by fax, or by mail using Form SS‑4 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4).

**2. What accounting method is required “with” an EIN?**  
* An EIN does **not** determine the accounting method you must use.  
* When you file your first income‑tax return, you choose an accounting method – either **cash** or **accrual** – and you may later request a change with Form 3115【Segment 1】【Segment 2】.  
* The choice is independent of whether you have an EIN; you can use either method for any entity that has an EIN.

So you need an EIN if your business falls into the situations above, and you still get to decide whether to use cash or accrual accounting when you file your first tax return.

1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

runs.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
runs.answer:
What to keep:  
- OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) – records each injury or illness that is “recordable.”  
- OSHA Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report) – a supplement that gives details for each recordable case.  
- OSHA Form 300A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) – the annual summary of the year’s recordable events.  

How long to keep them:  
- All of these OSHA records must be kept at the worksite for **at least five years** after the date of the injury.

runs.question: do i need workers comp insurance and can i deduct it
runs.answer:
Yes. Workers’ compensation insurance is required by state law for businesses that have employees, and the premiums you pay for it are deductible as a business expense on your Schedule C (Form 1040).  

- The IRS states that “Workers’ compensation insurance set by state law … is deductible.”[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37)  
- State‑level guidance also recommends that you carry workers’ compensation insurance to avoid civil lawsuits, implying it is effectively mandatory for employers with workers.[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9)

runs.question: what if a customer cannot get through my front door and what if someone is hurt on site
runs.answer:
**If a customer cannot get through the front door**

- The entrance must provide at least a **36‑inch clear width** when fully open; if older doors are narrower (e.g., 32 inches), the opening can be enlarged or a “swing‑clear” hinge can be added to give about 1½ extra inches of clearance. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)  
- Hand‑rail or round knob hardware that requires a tight grasp should be replaced with a lever handle or modified with a clamp‑on lever; a thumb latch can be disabled or removed so the door can be pulled open without depress‑ing the latch. These changes are usually inexpensive and quick to implement. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)  
- If the front door itself cannot be made accessible, provide an **alternative entrance** that is accessibility‑ready: a ramp, a door‑swinging from the opposite side, or a lift. The alternative entrance must be open during business hours. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)  
- When an alternative entrance exists, a clear sign directing customers to it must be posted. The sign must be in an accessible location and height. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  
- If a security turnstile blocks entry, remove the turnstile or replace it with an accessible gate so a minimum of 32 inches is available for wheelchair passage. The alternative entrance may also be achieved by using an exit door without a turnstile. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)  
- Update the business **policy** so that it does not exclude people with disabilities from entering, and allow service animals to accompany customers with disabilities. If a locked entrance exists during business hours, install an accessible call box or buzzer to unlock the door. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18)  

**If someone is hurt on site**

The supplied segments do not provide specific guidance on onsite injuries, first aid, or emergency medical response. Therefore, the answer to this part cannot be supplied from the available context.  
INSUFFICIENT

runs.question: how much cash before i have to report it and do i need a licence to serve food
runs.answer:
You must file a **Form 8300, Report of Cash Payments Over $10,000** if your business receives **more than $10,000 in cash in one transaction or in two or more related business transactions**. The definition of “cash” includes U.S. and foreign coin and currency, cashier’s and traveler’s checks, and money orders [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9).

---

### Food service licensing

If you are **preparing and serving food**, you need a license. An inspection must be completed first, and **approval from the State Health Department is required before a food license (or lodging license) is issued** [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=8). Therefore, **yes, a license is required** to serve food.

runs.question: why should i bother with a safety program and what records do i need to keep
runs.answer:
**Why a safety program matters**

1. A safety and health program is a proactive way to keep workers out of injury, illness, or death. The goal is to *prevent* events that would otherwise force you to deal with loss, litigation, and higher insurance costs. Investing in safety “now will help you avoid possible losses in the future” and makes a “safe business a sound business” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6).

2. Employers who make safety a daily part of operations see real benefits: *reduced injury and illness rates, fewer lost work days, lower workers’‑comp costs, and better worker morale* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90).

3. A written program demonstrates good‑faith commitment to worker health—a requirement for many participation and recognition programs (e.g., OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation Program, SHARP) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90).

**Key records you must keep (OSHA requirements)**

| Record type | What it includes | Retention period / reporting deadline | Where to get it |
|-------------|-----------------|----------------------------------------|-----------------|
| **OSHA Form 300** – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses | All injuries/illnesses that are *recordable* (see OSHA definition). | Keep on site for **at least five years** [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) and in many cases longer if required for specific industries. | OSHA’s website (Form 300, 300A, 301) |
| **OSHA Form 301** – Injury and Illness Incident Report | Detailed description of each *recordable* incident.  | Maintain a supplementary record for every case. | OSHA’s website |
| **OSHA Form 300A** – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses | Annual summary of the year’s injuries/illnesses. | Post the summary during February‑April and keep it on file for **five years**. | OSHA’s website |
| **Fatality, hospitalization, amputation, eye‑loss** | Must be reported **within 24 hours** (amputations, eye‑loss) and **within 8 hours** for fatalities. | Ongoing reporting each incident; keep the record for the retention period above. | OSHA’s reporting tool |
| **Worker medical and exposure records** | Medical records for occupational medical conditions and exposure logs. | Retain for the **time period** required for each specific record type (OSHA 1910.1020) [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15). | Company medical records |
| **Worker training records** | Records of training on hazard identification, control, and specific OSHA programs. | Keep **accessible for review by employees** as required by OSHA [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15). | Company HR/Training department |
| **Electronic submissions** (for large, high‑hazard employers) | OSHA Form 300, 301 data must be electronically submitted *annually by March 2* of the year after the covered calendar year if you have ≥100 workers in a high‑hazard industry. | Electronic filing deadline: **March 2**. | OSHA’s e‑recordkeeping portal |

**Who must keep records?**

* Employers are *partially exempt* if they had ten or fewer workers all year or if they are in a low‑hazard industry (29 CFR 1904.1 and Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A) [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).  
* All employers—regardless of size or industry—must record and report **fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, and eye‑loss** [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).

**Additional record‑keeping notes**

* Keep **written procedures and incident analysis logs** for near‑misses and workplace violence to evaluate and improve the program [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=85).  
* Maintain a **rescue telephone list** and emergency contact info visibly posted [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=13).  
* For infection control, record work‑related infectious diseases on Forms 300/301 and report fatalities or hospitalizations as above [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=48).

**Bottom line**  
A safety program protects workers, saves money by reducing injuries and insurance costs, enhances your business reputation, and keeps you compliant with OSHA’s record‑keeping statutes—most of which require keeping Form 300, 301, and 300A for five years, promptly reporting severe incidents, and maintaining training and medical records per OSHA’s timelines.

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
**How long you must keep tax records**

| Record type | Minimum retention period | Source |
|-------------|--------------------------|--------|
| Records that support a particular item of income or deduction on a tax return (e.g., receipts, invoices, bank statements) | Keep them until the “period of limitations” for that return has expired. The period of limitations is the time in which you can amend the return to claim a credit or refund, or in which the IRS can assess additional tax. If no other rule applies, the period of limitations is measured from the filing date of the return. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Copies of the completed tax return itself | Keep them forever; they help with future returns and with amended returns. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Employment‑tax records (W‑2s, payroll records, etc.) | Keep them for **at least 4 years** after the date the tax became due or was paid—whichever is later. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Asset‑related records (for depreciation, amortization, basis, gain/loss) | Keep them until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of that property. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Other specific records mentioned in separate publications | For example, records for a property disposed in a taxable disposition or for a non‑taxable exchange, retain records enough to compute depreciation, amortization, or basis. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

**Key take‑away**

- For most ordinary income‑tax documents, the retention time is the applicable period of limitations (often **3 years** from the filing date, but it can be longer if you’re claiming a loss or making an adjustment).  
- Employment‑tax documents require a longer window (**4 years**).  
- Asset‑related documents stay on file until the period of limitations ends for the year you sell, trade, or otherwise dispose of the property.  
- Always keep copies of your filed tax returns.

These guidelines come directly from the IRS rule‑making shown in Segment 1 and provide the specific figures and deadlines the documents themselves use.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
Business records help you manage and protect your business in several concrete ways:

1. **Show you how the business is doing** – By keeping detailed records you can see whether profits are growing, which products sell best, and what changes need to be made. This monitoring increases the likelihood of success. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

2. **Let you prepare accurate financial statements** – Records form the basis of income‑statement (profit‑and‑loss) and balance‑sheet reports that banks, creditors, and you need to review the business’s financial health. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

3. **Separate business and personal income** – The receipts you record identify where money comes from so you can distinguish taxable business income from non‑business or personal funds. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

4. **Capture deductible expenses** – Recording expenses as they occur prevents you from forgetting items that can reduce taxable income. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

5. **Support your tax returns** – Tax‑supporting documents (receipts, invoices, checkbooks) are required to prove the income, expenses, and credits reported on your returns. The IRS may request these records for inspection. A complete set speeds up any examination. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

6. **Meet record‑keeping requirements** – The IRS requires that records which support an item of income or deduction be kept until the applicable statute of limitations expires (usually until the period after the return is filed). Employment‑tax, asset, and inventory records also have specific retention periods. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

7. **Maintain a reliable accounting system** – Whether you use a manual book, electronic system, or computer software, the system must provide a clear, legible summary of all transactions and the ability to retrieve records for the IRS. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)

By keeping thorough, organized records, you can manage day‑to‑day operations, demonstrate compliance, protect yourself legally, and make the tax process smoother.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
When you start a business you pick one main accounting method—**cash** or **accrual**—and use it on your return and in your books.  
* Cash method: report income when you receive it and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you pay them. This is usually fine if you are a small business that does not keep inventory.  
* Accrual method: report income when you earn it (even if you don’t get paid yet) and match expenses with the year you incur them. If your business holds inventory (goods for sale, raw materials, etc.), the IRS requires the accrual method for purchases and sales. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

You can also combine methods, but the combination must behave exactly like the cash method or the accrual method for all income and expenses, and inventory still forces accrual for those items. If you want to change your method later you will need IRS approval, usually by filing Form 3115. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

**Bottom line:**  
* Use **cash** if you have no inventory and your business is simple.  
* Use **accrual** if you keep inventory or expect a more complex accounting picture.  
* If you want a hybrid, make sure it meets the IRS’s combination‑method rules.  

This guidance follows the IRS instructions for choosing and changing an accounting method.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards you can follow the steps below, all of which are described in the handbook sections you have:

1. **Do a routine self‑inspection**  
   - Knowledgeable employees should walk the shop floor and look for possible dangers.  
   - The handbook gives a **self‑inspection checklist** that covers general industry workplaces (not construction or maritime) and shows where to start when adding controls.  
   - After each inspection you record any hazards you find and note how they will be fixed.  
   – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Match what you see with OSHA standards**  
   - Review the standards that apply to your type of work, your equipment, and your materials.  
   - If a standard exists for a hazard, it usually takes priority over the general duty clause.  
   – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)

3. **Compile related data**  
   - Bring the completed checklists together with your injury/illness logs, training records, maintenance logs, and any incident reports.  
   - Looking at all of that information helps you spot patterns and decide where the biggest risks are.  
   – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

4. **Use available resources and external help**  
   - OSHA’s **On‑Site Consultation Program** offers free, confidential visits by trained specialists who can help you spot hazards and suggest fixes.  
   - If you need a deeper dive, the state‑wide consultation programs and local OSHA offices can answer questions about which standards apply or how to interpret them.  
   – [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)

5. **Check specific areas that often contain hazards**  
   * **Confining spaces** – confirm that the required signs, permits, tests, and lock‑out devices are in place before workers enter.  
   * **Work walkways** – keep surfaces clean, free of spills, and clear of obstructions; keep guardrails above 4 ft, and ensure proper lighting.  
   – [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=66), [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79), [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)

6. **Document and review**  
   - Record every finding and the action taken to control it.  
   - Review your safety program at least annually (or more often if needed) to ensure that the controls stay effective.  
   – [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=10)

**Bottom line:** Walk through your workplace, use the self‑inspection checklists, cross‑check with OSHA standards, collect and compare your incident data, and, if needed, get help from the OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program. These steps will help you spot, evaluate, and eliminate hazards.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash‑basis accounting records income and expenses only when money actually moves, while accrual‑basis accounting records them when they are earned or incurred, regardless of when cash is exchanged.  

* **Cash method** – you report income in the year you receive it and you normally deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you pay them. The IRS notes that this method is common for owners who have no inventory, because it is easier to track [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  

* **Accrual method** – you report income in the year you earn it (the customer’s right to pay is settled) and you deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you incur them, even if payment occurs later. The purpose is to match related income and expenses in the same year [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  

* **Inventory rule** – if you keep inventory (goods held for sale, raw materials, supplies that become part of merchandise), the IRS generally requires you to use the accrual method for purchases and sales, regardless of whether you otherwise might use cash [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  

* **Practical example** – a contractor who bills a client in December but receives the check in January will count that payment as income for the year the prize is received under cash method, but he will count it as income for the year the work was performed under accrual method [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  

Thus, cash method ties bookkeeping to the timing of cash flow, while accrual method ties it to the timing of economic events.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes – you may deduct the ordinary and necessary costs that are directly related to a business trip. The deductions are broken down by type of expense: | Type of expense | What is deductible (from the segments) | How to calculate | Relevant segment(s) | |-----------------|----------------------------------------|------------------|---------------------| | **Meals** | 50 % of the cost of meals you buy while traveling. You can also use the IRS standard meal allowance instead of actual costs. | If you use actual costs, multiply the total by 0.50. runs.question: what goes in an executive summary
runs.answer:
An executive summary is the short, front‑page overview of your business plan.  
It should be **one or two paragraphs**, written last after the rest of the plan is finished, and it must:

* **Explain the business idea** – what you’re offering and why it matters.  
* **State the financial need** – how much money you require, what you will do with it, and any money you’ve already invested.  
* **Outline a brief schedule of goals** – key milestones you expect to hit as the business grows.

In short, it gives a quick snapshot of the plan’s main points so a reader can grasp the opportunity, funding request, and timeline without reading the entire document. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
To describe your target market, follow the guidance in the planning material:

1. **Define the market niche** – Identify the group of customers who are most likely to buy your product or service.  
   - Explain who your “best” customer is.  
   - Describe their key characteristics.  
   - For business markets, you might segment by industry, company size, location, or product use/application.  
   - For consumer markets, you could segment by demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application, or benefits sought.  
   - [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Estimate the size and growth potential** –  
   - Use population figures, sales tax data, industry reports, or other reliable sources to approximate the total size of the segment.  
   - Estimate how much of that total market you expect to capture.  
   - [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Illustrate with examples** –  
   - Provide concrete, specific examples that show how the market segment would interact with your offering.  
   - [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

In short, describe who they are, why they would buy your product, and how many of them you can realistically reach and win over.



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes.  Under the ADA you are required to make a shop that serves the public “readily achievable” accessible to people who use wheelchairs.  That means:

* **Remove any physical barriers that are readily achievable** – the law specifically requires that any barrier that can be fixed or altered with reasonable effort and without undue expense be removed [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).  
* **Provide at least one accessible entrance** – if you have more than one public entrance you can make only one of them accessible, but it must be usable by a wheelchair.  If a second entrance is not accessible, you must post a sign that directs customers to the accessible one [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  
* **Give an accessible route from the sidewalk/parking to that entrance** – the route must be level, have no steps or steep slopes, and have a firm, stable, slip‑resistant surface [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  
* **Adjust doors, counters, and other fixtures so they are usable in a wheelchair** – this can include installing a lever handle, adding a threshold‑free entry, lowering counters to no more than 34 inches, and providing a clear 30‑in × 48‑in space in front of each counter [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  

If a barrier or modification is not “readily achievable” (for example, it would require a major structural change), the ADA allows you to offer alternative services (home delivery, curb‑side pickup, etc.) [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/322-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  In short, you must make your shop wheelchair‑accessible to the extent that it is reasonably possible to do so.



**Sources:**

runs.question: how long do i have to report a workplace death
runs.answer:
All work‑related fatalities must be reported to OSHA within **8 hours** of the incident.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)



**Sources:**

runs.question: when do i report an amputation to osha
runs.answer:
You must notify OSHA of any work‑related amputation **within 24 hours** of the incident.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=48)

If the amputation resulted in a fatality, that would be required within 8 hours, but the specific deadline for an amputation alone is the 24‑hour window.

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
You may be *partially exempt* from OSHA’s injury‑and‑illness recordkeeping rules, but you still have some reporting duties.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

**When the exemption applies**

| Criterion | Exemption status | Remarks |
|----------|------------------|--------|
| 10 or fewer workers during **every calendar year of the previous year** | ✔ | This is the most common exception. |
| Employer is in a **low‑hazard industry** listed in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A | ✔ | Only certain industries qualify. |

**What you still must do even if exempt**

- All employers (exempt or not) must report **work‑related fatalities** to OSHA within 8 hours, and **in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye** within 24 hours.  
- If your business has **100 or more workers in a designated high‑hazard industry**, you must electronically submit OSHA Forms 300, 301, and 300A by **March 2 of the year after the calendar year covered**.  
- In addition, injury/illness records (OSHA 300, 300A, and 301) must be kept on the worksite for at least **five years** if you are *not* exempt.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

So, if your company had 10 or fewer employees last year or fits into the low‑hazard industry list, you’re exempt from keeping the day‑to‑day OSHA injury and illness logs, but you still must report fatalities and severe injuries and keep any required records for the five‑year period if you fall under the higher‑worker or high‑hazard rules.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: how long do i keep injury records
runs.answer:
Injury and illness records (OSHA Forms 300, 300A, and 301) must be kept at the worksite for **at least five years**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
runs.answer:
**Tax‑related records**

| Record type | How long to keep | Source |
|-------------|------------------|--------|
| General business books, receipts, invoices, and other documents that support income, expenses, deductions, or credits on a tax return | **Until the period of limitation for that return expires** – usually the time during which you could amend the return or the IRS could assess additional tax (Table 3 in the publication). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Copies of filed tax returns | Indefinitely, because they help prepare future returns and are needed if the IRS requests them. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Employment‑tax records (e.g., Forms 941, 940, payroll registers) | **At least 4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Asset‑related records (purchase, sale, depreciation, etc.) | Keep until the period of limitation expires for the year in which the asset is disposed of. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

**Injury‑related records**

| Record type | How long to keep | Source |
|-------------|------------------|--------|
| OSHA Form 300 (log of work‑related injuries and illnesses) | **At least 5 years from the end of the calendar year that the record was completed** (i.e., kept at the worksite for five years). | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| OSHA Form 301 (incident reports for recordable injuries/illnesses) | Same as Form 300 – keep at the worksite for **at least 5 years**. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| OSHA Form 300A (annual summary) | Not an individual injury record; no specific retention period stated in the segments. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) |

**Summary**

- Keep all tax‑related documents until the relevant limitation period ends, with employment‑tax records for a minimum of four years and asset records until the limitation period for that year expires.  
- Keep OSHA injury logs (Form 300) and detailed incident reports (Form 301) on the worksite for at least five years.  

These durations are those explicitly set in the provided segments.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)
2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)
3. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)
