runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
The segments do provide information that allows you to answer the question.  

**Do you need an EIN?**  
You need an Employer Identification Number (EIN) under the following circumstances:  
* if you hire employees — or have a payroll to run [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
* if you file certain federal tax returns such as payroll, excise, or certain excise tax returns [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
* many business structures (partnerships, LLCs, corporations) are required to obtain an EIN, and a sole‑proprietor may choose to get one to keep the owner’s Social‑Security number separate from the business ID [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)  
If you are a sole proprietor with no employees and you are happy to use your Social‑Security number for all federal filings, you could optionally skip the EIN, but many IRS publications recommend it so the business has a distinct taxpayer ID [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4).

**What accounting method goes with an EIN?**  
An EIN itself does not “come with” a particular accounting method.  
When you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (or other business form), you must choose an accounting method—cash, accrual, or a combination that clearly shows income [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  
You can use the same method for all purposes (tax, bookkeeping, and reporting) and you must keep records that make the method clear. The choice is independent of whether you have an EIN.  

So:  
* You likely need an EIN if you have employees or any of the business structures listed above.  
* The accounting method is chosen when you file your first return and it is not dictated by having an EIN.  

These statements are drawn from the excerpts in Segments 1, 2, 3, and 4.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 6)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/324-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

runs.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
runs.answer:
For workplace injuries you must keep the OSHA injury‑recording forms:

- **OSHA Form 300** – the log of work‑related injuries and illnesses.  
- **OSHA Form 301** – the detailed incident report for each recordable case.  
- **OSHA Form 300A** – the annual summary of all injuries and illnesses for the calendar year.  
(Employers may use equivalent forms that contain the same required information.) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

And you must retain those records for **at least five years** after the date they are created, keeping them at the worksite. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: do i need workers comp insurance and can i deduct it
runs.answer:
Yes. If you have employees, most states require that you carry workers’ compensation insurance; the Department of Labor recommends it to avoid civil lawsuits [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9).  

You can also deduct the premiums you pay for workers’ compensation as a business expense.  The IRS treats workers’ compensation insurance as deductible (and lists it among the types of insurance premiums that are generally deductible) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37).  In expense planning tables, workers’ comp is listed explicitly as an expense you can include on Schedule C and deduct as a normal business cost [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=19).

runs.question: how much cash before i have to report it and do i need a licence to serve food
runs.answer:
The information in the provided segments does answer both parts of your question.

**1. Cash reporting threshold**  
You only need to file a tax‑reporting form when you receive **more than $10,000 in one transaction or in two or more related business transactions**. The IRS requires you to file Form 8300 for that cash receipt [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/323-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12).

**2. License to serve food**  
If you are preparing and serving food, you must first have a health‑department inspection and get the Health Department’s approval **before you are issued a food license** (or a lodging license) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=8). Depending on your city or county, you may also need a local permit, so it’s a good idea to contact the local jurisdiction for any additional requirements [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/326-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=7).

runs.question: why should i bother with a safety program and what records do i need to keep
runs.answer:
Because a safety program is more than a box‑check exercise – it protects the people who run your business, keeps the business running smoothly, and helps you avoid costly surprises.

**Why a safety program matters**  
- It keeps workers from injuries, illnesses, and deaths, which saves money, protects families and keeps the business operating – a “safe business is a sound business.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6)  
- It shifts the focus from fixing problems after they happen to finding and eliminating hazards first, which is far more effective and less disruptive. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  
- It lets you demonstrate “good faith and commitment” to OSHA, making it easier to work with consultants, insurers and regulators, and often reduces costs such as workers’ compensation. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  
- OSHA’s records, reports, and inspections confirm that you’ve done your due diligence and can help avoid penalties and litigation. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  

**What records you must keep**

| Record type | What it covers | How long to keep | Where to file | Key deadlines |
|-------------|---------------|-----------------|---------------|---------------|
| **OSHA Form 300 – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses** | Every injury or illness that is not a simple first‑aid case | At least 5 years | On‑site (paper or electronic) |  |
| **OSHA Form 301 – Injury and Illness Incident Report** | Detailed incident information for each recordable case | At least 5 years | On‑site (paper or electronic) |  |
| **OSHA Form 300A – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses** | Annual summary prepared from Forms 300 and 301 | At least 5 years | On‑site (paper or electronic) | Submit electronically by **March 2 of the year after** the calendar year covered, if you have 100 or more workers in a high‑hazard industry. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) |
| **Fatality, hospitalization, amputation, or eye‑loss reports** | Must be reported to OSHA immediately | Retain the original report and corrective‑action summary for as long as the OSHA record‑keeping period (5 years) | On‑site | Report within **8 hours** for fatalities; within **24 hours** for hospitalizations, amputations, or loss of an eye. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker medical and exposure records** | Records required in the industry (e.g., exposure logs, medical evaluations) | Retain for the period required by the specific record (usually as long as the employee is exposed) | On‑site (paper or electronic) | As required by 29 CFR 1910.1020. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker training records** | Proof that employees received the required safety and health training | Keep these records at the worksite and make them accessible to workers | On‑site (paper or electronic) | As required by the relevant OSHA standard. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

**Other useful records**  
- Hazard identification and assessment logs, safety inspection checklists, and near‑miss reports can help you spot trends and design prevention measures (see Segment 8 for the business‑side view of keeping all records).  
- If you participate in OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation or Safety & Health Achievement Recognition Program, keep the consultant reports and safety‑achievement certificates. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)  
- For high‑risk industries that have special recording rules, be sure to check 29 CFR Part 1904 or the corresponding state‑plan guidance. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/325-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)  

**Bottom line**  
A safety program helps you avoid fatal accidents, keeps you compliant with OSHA reporting laws, and saves money on insurance and lost‑time costs. The records listed above are the ones required by OSHA, and keeping them for the proper time and in the proper place lets you prove you’re doing the right thing if an inspection or claim comes through.

runs.question: how do i register a trademark
runs.answer:
To register a trademark you can choose either a state‑level or a federal filing.  
The basic steps are:

1. **Decide the level of protection** –  
   * State‑level registration gives you exclusive rights within the state you file.  
   * Federal registration (via the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, USPTO) gives you nationwide rights.  

2. **Check if the mark is available** – Search the relevant trademark databases (state database or the USPTO’s TESS system) to make sure no identical or confusingly similar mark is already registered.  

3. **Prepare and file the application** –  
   * For a state filing, submit an application to the Secretary of State office in the state where you want protection.  
   * For a federal filing, submit an application to the USPTO.  

4. **Pay the filing fee** – Each jurisdiction sets its own fee schedule (the USPTO has standard fees listed on its website).  

5. **Wait for examination** – The office will review the application. If issues are found, you’ll receive a correspondence (office action) with instructions on how to proceed.  

6. **Publication and registration** – If the USPTO accepts the application, the mark is published in the *Trademark Official Gazette* and, after the opposition period expires without complaint, the trademark is registered. For a state filing, the Office of the Secretary of State will issue a registration certificate.

**Contacts**

* Secretary of State (state filing) – (605) 773‑2797 or https://sdsos.gov/  
* U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (federal filing) – (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199; https://www.uspto.gov  

These are the actionable steps and contact points for registering a trademark.
